"Put out" is a phrasal verb — a combination of a verb ("put") and a small word ("out") that together create a new meaning, often very different from the individual words alone. It's one of the most versatile phrasal verbs in English, with many distinct meanings. The correct meaning always depends on context.
1. To Extinguish (a Fire, Flame, or Light)

This is the most literal and common meaning. When you "put out" a fire, you stop it from burning.

Examples:

  • "The firefighters put out the fire in an hour."
  • "Please put out your cigarette before entering."
  • "She put out the candles after dinner."

Think of it this way: a fire is "going." You push it "out of existence." You put it out.
2. To Cause Inconvenience to Someone

If you "put someone out," you cause them trouble, extra effort, or discomfort — usually by asking them to do something for you.

Examples:

  • "I don't want to put you out — I can manage on my own."
  • "He felt bad about putting his hosts out by arriving so late."
  • "Am I putting you out if I ask you to pick me up?"

This is a polite and common phrase. When someone says "please don't put yourself out," they mean: "please don't go to any extra trouble for me."
3. To Feel Annoyed or Bothered (Adjective Form)

When someone is put out, they feel irritated, offended, or upset — usually because they were inconvenienced or disrespected.

Examples:

  • "She was quite put out when no one thanked her for cooking."
  • "He seemed put out by the last-minute change of plans."
  • "I could tell she was put out, even though she didn't say anything."

Notice the structure here: "to be put out" (adjective). The person feels a mild, simmering annoyance — not explosive anger, but quiet frustration or hurt pride.
4. To Release, Publish, or Produce Something

When a company, artist, or organization "puts out" something, they release or publish it for the public.

Examples:

  • "The band put out their third album last year."
  • "The government put out an official statement this morning."
  • "The company put out a new version of their software."
  • "She has put out three novels since 2020."

This is very commonly used in journalism, music, business, and entertainment. It simply means: to send something out into the world.
5. To Place Something Outside / To Make Someone Leave

When you put something — or someone — "out," you move them to the outside, away from an interior space.

Examples:

  • "Could you put out the rubbish before you go to bed?" (take the trash outside)
  • "She put the cat out every night." (let the cat outside)
  • "He was put out of the game for fighting." (removed/ejected)

This is very common in British English for tasks like taking out the bins (garbage cans).
6. To Extend a Body Part

When you "put out" your hand, foot, or arm, you stretch or extend it outward.

Examples:

  • "He put out his hand to introduce himself."
  • "She put out her foot and tripped him accidentally."
  • "The officer put out his arm to stop the crowd."

This is a simple, physical use — you are projecting a part of your body outward.
7. To Produce or Generate (Power, Energy, or Output)

Machines, engines, or systems can "put out" a certain amount of energy, heat, or power.

Examples:

  • "This engine puts out 300 horsepower."
  • "The heater puts out enough warmth for the whole room."
  • "How much electricity does this solar panel put out?"

This is technical but very commonly used in everyday conversation when talking about machines or devices.
8. To Dislocate a Part of Your Body

If you "put out" your shoulder, your knee, or your back, you injure it by displacing it from its normal position.

Examples:

  • "He put out his back lifting those heavy boxes."
  • "She put out her shoulder during the game."
  • "Be careful — you'll put out your knee jumping like that."

This use is especially common in British and Australian English.
9. To Set Sail / Leave a Port (Nautical)

A ship or boat "puts out" when it departs from shore and heads out to sea.

Examples:

  • "The fishing boats put out at dawn."
  • "The ship put out from the harbor despite the storm warnings."

This is a traditional seafaring expression. You may encounter it in literature, news, or conversations about sailing.
10. In Baseball: To Retire a Batter or Runner

In baseball, when a fielder causes a batter or runner to be declared "out," we say the player was "put out." The noun form is a putout.

Example:

  • "The shortstop put out the runner at second base."
  • "He had three putouts in that inning."
11. The Informal/Slang Meaning (Adults)

In informal, casual American English, "put out" can refer to someone being willing to have sex. It is considered slang and is typically used in a crude or blunt way.

Example:

  • "He complained that she wouldn't put out."

You will encounter this in movies, TV shows, and casual conversation. It is not polite or formal language. Knowing it helps you understand what people mean when you hear or read it in informal contexts.
Grammar: How "Put Out" Works

Separable phrasal verb: In most of its meanings, the object (the noun) can go either between "put" and "out," or after "out."

  • "Put out the fire." ✅
  • "Put the fire out." ✅

However, when the object is a pronoun (it, him, her, them), it must go in the middle:

  • "Put it out." ✅
  • "Put out it." ❌

Intransitive use (no object): In a few meanings — especially the nautical use and the slang use — "put out" needs no object.

  • "The ship put out." ✅ (no object needed)
Quick Summary of All Meanings

• Extinguish → Put out a fire/candle/light
  • Inconvenience → I hope I'm not putting you out
  • Feel annoyed → She was put out by his behavior
  • Release/publish → The artist put out a new song
  • Place outside → Put out the trash / put the cat out
  • Extend a body part → He put out his hand
  • Generate power → The engine puts out 400 horsepower
  • Dislocate → She put out her shoulder
  • Depart by sea → The ship put out at sunrise
  • Baseball retirement → The runner was put out at third
  • Slang (adult) → Willing to have sex (crude, informal)

The key to mastering "put out" — like all phrasal verbs — is context. Once you notice whether the speaker is talking about a fire, a person's feelings, a ship, a machine, or a music album, the meaning will almost always be obvious.
